analysis.one_liner: Lets unions require workers to join and pay dues, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2014 with 29 Democratic sponsors and cosponsors, referred to committee, and died there with no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently lets states pass 'right-to-work' laws that bar union contracts requiring workers to join the union or pay dues. This bill would delete that provision, so unions and employers could negotiate union-security agreements in every state, including states whose laws currently ban them.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in unionized workplaces and labor unions gain: unions could collect dues from all workers they represent, which typically increases their resources for bargaining, and represented workers receive the benefits of union contracts whether or not they choose to join. Union membership and funding would likely rise in the roughly half of states with right-to-work laws.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the provision that lets states prohibit agreements requiring union membership as a condition of employment.

With that provision gone, unions and employers could negotiate union-security contracts everywhere, allowing unions to require all workers they represent to join and pay dues, which strengthens union finances and bargaining power.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls mainly on non-union workers in unionized workplaces, who could no longer keep their jobs without joining the union and paying dues, and on employers who face stronger unions with more negotiating leverage. States lose the power to set this policy themselves.

drawbacks.text: Workers who prefer not to join a union would lose that choice in unionized workplaces: they would have to pay dues as a condition of employment, which right-to-work supporters view as a matter of individual freedom.
The bill overrides state law in roughly half the states that have chosen to ban mandatory union dues, taking away a policy decision those states made for themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Stronger unions generally raise pay and benefits for the workers they represent, and requiring dues from all represented workers funds that bargaining. The real trade-off is individual choice: workers who would rather not join or pay would lose that option, and states that deliberately chose right-to-work rules would have that choice taken away. The bill was a one-sided statement of the pro-union position and never got a hearing, so no compromise version was ever developed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, and the Congress ended two weeks later without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on December 11, 2014, with 28 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and their allies who oppose mandatory union dues are better off: a bill that would have let unions require dues in every state died without even a hearing. Non-union workers who prefer not to pay dues also keep the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers opposed to mandatory union dues

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to allow union-security agreements in all states.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 11, 2014 and took no further action; it never received a hearing or vote.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled committee action on the bill, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee and House took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill would let unions require dues from every worker they represent in all 50 states, substantially increasing union membership and revenue, which unions use to bargain for higher pay and benefits for those workers.
Employers, especially in right-to-work states, would face stronger unions with more funds and full-member bargaining units, increasing labor costs and reducing management flexibility.
